A past-tense verb with the 'we' ending built into its shape, so no separate pronoun is needed. This particular verb works like 'to be', setting up a past state and inviting the rest of the sentence to say where or how the group was.

A preposition meaning 'with / in the company of', placing the following noun in the genitive. It marks accompaniment, linking the speakers to the person they were alongside, and it heads into a possessive chain naming exactly who that was.

A noun in the genitive (because the preposition before it governs that) that opens a possessive pairing with the divine name after it. It owns the next word in an 'X of Y' chain, and the genitive ending is what links the two without a separate 'of'.

The divine name in the genitive as the owner half of the possessive pairing before it: 'the messenger of God'. Set directly after the first noun with no separate word for 'of', its genitive ending supplies that link and makes the whole title definite.

A past-tense verb opening the standard blessing on the Prophet. It carries 'he' inside its form, and grammatically the divine name right after it is its subject, so the phrase reads 'God blessed (him)'. This is a fixed honorific formula.

The divine name standing as the subject of the blessing verb before it, in the nominative as the doer. Within this honorific formula it is the one who sends the blessing, not part of a possessive chain here.

A preposition meaning 'upon' fused with a 'him' pronoun, completing the first half of the blessing as 'upon him'. The attached pronoun points to the Prophet, and the pair marks who the blessing settles on.

The wa- on the front is the linking 'and', adding the second half of the blessing. The verb that follows means 'grant peace', carrying its subject inside, so the whole formula reads 'and granted (him) peace'. This is a set honorific phrase.

A preposition meaning 'in/at' that places the following noun in the genitive, marking the setting of the gathering. It locates the whole scene, telling you the circumstance in which they were together.

An indefinite noun (it carries the -in tanwin, not al-) in the genitive after the preposition before it. Its indefiniteness presents the occasion as an unspecified one, and the genitive ending is forced by the 'at' preposition governing it.

The connector fa- 'so/then' fused to a passive verb. Fa- marks this as the next step in the scene, and the verb is passive: the foreleg was brought to him by someone left unnamed, with the passive shown by the vowel pattern inside the verb rather than a helper word.

A preposition meaning 'to/toward' fused with a 'him' pronoun, marking the direction of the presenting. The whole 'to him' is one word, and the attached pronoun points to the Prophet as the one it was brought to.

A noun made definite by al- 'the', standing as the subject of the passive verb before it: it is the thing that 'was presented'. With a passive verb the thing receiving the action becomes the grammatical subject, so its nominative ending marks it here.

The wa- on the front is the linking 'and'. The verb that follows is a past 'was' form carrying a feminine ending that agrees with the foreleg; it sets up an ongoing past state, leading into 'used to please him'.

A present-tense verb with an 'it' subject and a 'him' pronoun fused on as its object. The verb's logic is reversed from English: the foreleg is the doer that 'pleases', and the 'him' is the one pleased, so the thing liked is grammatically the actor.

The connector fa- 'so/then' fused to a past-tense verb. Fa- ties this biting to the previous step as what came next, and the verb carries 'he' inside its shape, stating the action and its doer in one word.

A preposition meaning 'from' fused with a feminine 'it' pronoun, marking the source of the bite. The whole 'from it' is one word, and the pronoun reaches back to the feminine 'foreleg' mentioned earlier rather than the nearest noun.

An indefinite noun in the accusative that counts the action: it specifies one instance of biting, the way English might say 'a single bite'. This accusative noun echoing the verb's own root is how Arabic pins down how much or how many times the action happened.
The wa- on the front is the linking 'and'. The verb that follows is past-tense with 'he' inside it and introduces direct speech, so what comes after is the quoted words rather than more narration.

A standalone 'I' pronoun. Arabic usually buries the subject inside the verb, so spelling out a separate 'I' here adds weight and contrast, stressing 'I myself' as the one making the claim that follows.

A noun that serves as the 'am' half of the sentence, the predicate paired with the 'I' before it; Arabic needs no verb 'to be' in the present, so the bare noun does that work. It also opens a possessive pairing, owning the noun after it.

A noun made definite by al- 'the', in the genitive as the owner half of the possessive pairing before it: 'the master of the people'. The two nouns sit directly together, and this genitive ending supplies the 'of' with no separate word.

A time noun in the accusative, pinning the claim to a specific occasion. The accusative is what turns it into a 'when' adverb, and it heads a possessive pairing with the noun after it, naming exactly which day.

A noun made definite by al- 'the', in the genitive as the owner half of the pairing before it: 'the day of the Resurrection'. Its definiteness fixes the whole phrase as one specific, known day, with the genitive ending supplying the 'of'.

A yes-or-no question particle. It carries no meaning of its own beyond flipping the following statement into a question, the way English inverts word order or adds 'do'. Its whole job is to signal that an answer is expected.

A present-tense verb with the 'you (plural)' ending built into its shape, addressing a group. The subject is carried inside the verb, so the single word asks 'do you (all) know' without a separate pronoun.

A fused question word formed from 'from' plus 'what', meaning 'from what / why'. The merging of the two pieces is a regular contraction, and together they ask after the cause or source of the thing being pointed to.

A demonstrative meaning 'that', pointing back to the situation just raised rather than to a physical object. It works as the topic the question is about, gathering up the preceding idea into a single 'that'.

A present-tense verb with 'he' built into its shape, opening the scene. The subject comes as a separate word right after it (a verb-first order Arabic prefers), so the verb stays singular and the doer is named in the following word.

The divine name standing as the subject of the verb before it, in the nominative as the doer of the gathering. Placed after its verb in the usual verb-first order, it is the word that actually names who acts.

A plural noun made definite by al- 'the', acting as the object of the gathering verb. Its accusative ending marks it as one of the things being gathered, the receiver of the action rather than the doer.

The wa- on the front is the linking 'and', pairing this group with the previous one as a second object. It too is a definite plural in the accusative, so the two together are what God gathers: the earliest and the latest.
A preposition meaning 'in' that places the following noun in the genitive, marking where the gathering happens. It locates the whole event in a single shared spot.

An indefinite noun (carrying the -in tanwin) in the genitive after the preposition before it. Its indefiniteness leaves the place unspecified, and the noun after it will narrow it down; the genitive ending is forced by the 'in'.

A number word 'one' working as an adjective on the place noun before it, matching it in being indefinite and genitive. It stresses that the whole of humanity is gathered into a single shared spot, so the count carries the point of unity.

The connector fa- 'so/then' fused to a present-tense verb. Fa- carries the narration forward to the next stage, and the verb holds 'he/they' inside it; the subject is named in the word right after, in verb-first order.
A noun made definite by al- 'the', the subject of the saying verb before it. Its nominative ending marks it as the speakers, named after the verb in the usual order.

A particle that turns the following statement into a rhetorical, urging question: 'do you not...?'. It blends a question with a nudge, expecting agreement rather than information, and colours the whole clause after it.

A present-tense verb with the 'you (plural)' ending built into its shape, addressing the crowd. The subject is folded into the verb, so the single word asks 'do you (all) see' without a separate pronoun.

A preposition meaning 'to/toward' that here directs attention, working with the seeing verb so the gaze is turned onto the following relative word. It puts what follows in the genitive and points the looking at it.
A relative word meaning 'what / that which', naming the state the people are in. It opens a clause that the following words fill out, standing in for the unnamed situation they are caught in.

A standalone 'you (plural)' pronoun, the subject inside the relative clause. Spelling it out as a separate word, rather than burying it in a verb, frames the bare 'you are' statement that the next word locates.

A preposition meaning 'in' fused with a 'it' pronoun, meaning 'in it'. The whole phrase is one word, and the pronoun points back to the state named by the relative word just before, closing the 'the state you are in' clause.

A preposition meaning 'to/toward' repeating the earlier directing word to add a second thing the gaze is turned onto. It governs the genitive on what follows and parallels the first 'look to', so the two phrases stack the things being pointed at.

A relative word meaning 'what / that which', here naming what has come upon the people. It heads a clause completed by the verb after it, standing in for the unspecified events that have befallen them.

A past-tense verb with a 'you (plural)' pronoun fused on as its object, meaning 'reached you'. The thing that arrives is the verb's subject, carried inside its form, while the attached 'you' is the one it overtook, so the people are grammatically the receivers.

A particle that frames the next words as an urging, rhetorical question, 'will you not...?'. It expects agreement rather than facts and shifts the appeal toward a plea, setting the tone for the request that follows.

A present-tense verb with the 'you (plural)' ending built into its shape, here meaning to seek out or look for. The subject sits inside the verb, and the verb takes the following word as the thing being sought.
An open relative pronoun meaning 'someone who / whoever', used for an unspecified person. It is the object of the seeking verb and at once opens a clause describing what that someone would do.

A present-tense verb with 'he' built into its shape, describing the action of the unnamed someone: to intercede. It heads the clause that defines the person being sought, telling you what they are wanted for.
The preposition li- 'for' fused with a 'you (plural)' pronoun, marking who the intercession would benefit. The whole 'for you' is one word, the attached pronoun pointing to the pleading crowd.

A preposition meaning 'to/toward' that here marks the one the intercession is directed at, putting the following noun in the genitive. It links the act of interceding to the Lord it is addressed before.

A noun with a 'your (plural)' pronoun fused onto its end, a possessive in one word. It stands in the genitive because the preposition before it governs that ending, and the attached 'your' stresses the crowd's own bond with their Lord.

The connector fa- 'so/then' fused to a present-tense verb. Fa- moves the narration to the next exchange, and the verb carries its subject inside; the doer is named in the word right after, in verb-first order.

A noun meaning 'some/part of' that heads a possessive pairing with the noun after it: 'some of the people'. It is the subject of the saying verb, and it owns the following genitive noun, carving a portion out of the whole crowd.

A noun made definite by al- 'the', in the genitive as the owner half of the pairing before it: 'some of the people'. The two nouns sit directly together, and this genitive ending supplies the 'of' that English spells out.

The preposition li- 'to' fused to an indefinite noun, meaning 'to others'. Li- marks the addressee of the speech and forces the genitive, while the indefinite noun (with its tanwin) leaves the 'others' unspecified, pairing with the earlier 'some' to mean group speaking to group.

A noun with a 'your (plural)' pronoun fused onto its end, a possessive in one word: 'your father'. It is what the speakers point to, and the attached 'your' addresses the whole crowd as descendants of the one named next.

A proper name standing in apposition to 'your father' just before it, spelling out who that father is. The two words refer to the same person, so this name simply pins down the identity of the noun it follows.
and they will go to him

Three pieces in one word: the connector wa- 'and', a present-tense verb, and a 'him' pronoun fused on as object. Wa- continues the action, the verb carries its 'they' subject inside, and the attached 'him' marks the figure they go to.

The connector fa- 'so/then' fused to a present-tense verb with the 'they' ending inside it. Fa- marks the saying as following straight from the going, and the subject is carried in the verb, so the word means 'so they say'.

A calling particle, the 'O' used to hail someone directly before naming them. It flags that what follows is a person being addressed, the way English 'O' or just direct address marks the start of speaking to someone.

A proper name standing as the one being called, right after the calling particle. It is the addressee of the speech, set in the form a vocative takes, so the words together open the direct address to him.

A standalone 'you' pronoun beginning a bare nominal sentence. Arabic needs no verb 'to be', so this 'you' plus the following noun already means 'you are...'; spelling out the pronoun also lays stress on him as the subject.

A noun serving as the 'are' half of the sentence, the predicate paired with the 'you' before it. It also heads a possessive pairing, owning the noun after it, so it sets up 'the father of...' to be completed next.

A noun made definite by al- 'the', in the genitive as the owner half of the pairing before it: 'the father of humankind'. The two nouns sit directly together, the genitive ending supplying the 'of' with no separate word.

A past-tense verb with a 'you' pronoun fused on as its object, meaning 'created you'. The verb carries its 'he' subject inside, and the divine name in the next word is that subject, so the attached 'you' is the one created.
The divine name standing as the subject of the creating verb before it, in the nominative as the doer. Placed after its verb in verb-first order, it names who performed the creation just stated.

The preposition bi- 'with' fused to a noun carrying a 'his' pronoun, all in one word. Bi- marks the means of the creating and forces the genitive, while the attached 'his' ties the hand back to God, the subject named just before.

The wa- on the front is the linking 'and', continuing God's actions. The past-tense verb carries 'he' inside it, so it reads 'and he breathed', keeping the same subject across the chain of deeds without restating it.
A preposition meaning 'in/into' fused with a 'you' pronoun, meaning 'into you'. The whole phrase is one word, and the attached pronoun marks Adam as the one the breath was placed into.

A preposition meaning 'from/of' used partitively, naming a portion of God's spirit as the source of the breath. It governs the following noun in the genitive and frames it as the wellspring of what was breathed in.

A noun with a 'his' pronoun fused onto its end, a possessive in one word. It stands in the genitive because the partitive preposition before it governs that ending, and the attached 'his' ties the spirit back to God.

The wa- on the front is the linking 'and', adding another of God's deeds. The past-tense verb carries 'he' inside it, so it reads 'and he commanded', the subject staying the same across the listed actions.
A noun made definite by al- 'the', the object of the commanding verb before it. Its accusative ending marks it as the ones commanded, the receivers of the order rather than the giver.

The connector fa- 'so/then' fused to a past-tense verb with the 'they' ending inside it. Fa- marks the prostration as the result of the command, so it reads 'so they prostrated', the subject carried in the verb.
The preposition li- 'to' fused with a 'you' pronoun, marking the one the prostration was directed toward. The whole 'to you' is one word, the attached pronoun pointing to Adam as its focus.

The wa- on the front is the linking 'and'. The past-tense verb carries 'he' inside it and a 'you' pronoun fused on as object, so it reads 'and he settled you', with God still the subject and Adam the one settled.

A noun made definite by al- 'the', the object marking where Adam was settled. Its accusative ending fits a verb of placing that takes the destination directly as an object, so 'in Paradise' is carried by the bare accusative noun.

A particle framing the next words as an urging, rhetorical question, 'will you not...?'. It expects agreement rather than information and turns the clause into a plea, colouring the whole request that follows.

A present-tense verb with 'you' built into its shape, addressing one person. The subject sits inside the verb, so the single word means 'you intercede', and under the urging particle before it the sense becomes 'won't you intercede'.
The preposition li- 'for' fused with a 'us' pronoun, marking who the interceding would benefit. The whole 'for us' is one word, the attached pronoun pointing to the pleading group.
A preposition meaning 'to/toward' that marks the one the intercession is addressed before, putting the following noun in the genitive. It links the act of interceding to the Lord it is brought to.

A noun with a 'your' (singular) pronoun fused onto its end, a possessive in one word. It stands in the genitive because the preposition before it governs that ending, and the attached 'your' stresses the addressee's own bond with his Lord.

A particle reopening the rhetorical, urging question, 'do you not...?'. Repeated here, it stacks a second appeal onto the first, expecting agreement and keeping the pleading tone across the following clause.
A present-tense verb with 'you' (singular) built into its shape, meaning to see or perceive. The subject is inside the verb, and under the urging particle before it the sense is 'do you not see'.

A relative word meaning 'what / that which', here naming the state the speakers are in. It is the object of the seeing verb and opens a clause completed by the next words, standing in for their unnamed plight.

A standalone 'we' pronoun, the subject inside the relative clause. Spelling it out as a separate word frames the bare 'we are' statement that the following 'in it' locates, since Arabic needs no verb 'to be' here.

A preposition meaning 'in' fused with a 'it' pronoun, meaning 'in it'. The pronoun points back to the state named by the relative word before, closing the 'the state we are in' clause in a single word.

Two pieces fused: the linking wa- 'and' plus a relative word meaning 'what / that which'. Wa- adds a second thing to be seen, and the relative word opens a clause naming what has come upon them, completed by the verb after it.

A past-tense verb with a 'us' pronoun fused on as its object, meaning 'reached us'. The thing that arrives is the verb's hidden subject, while the attached 'us' is the one it overtook, so the speakers are grammatically the receivers.

A particle framing the next words as an urging, rhetorical question, 'do you not...?'. It expects agreement rather than facts and colours the whole clause as a plea, setting up the appeal that follows.
A present-tense verb with 'you' (singular) built into its shape, meaning to see. The subject is inside the verb, and under the urging particle before it the sense becomes 'do you not see'.

A relative word meaning 'what / that which', naming the state the speakers are in. It is the object of the seeing verb and opens a clause completed by the following words, standing in for their unnamed plight.
A standalone 'we' pronoun, the subject inside the relative clause. Spelling it out frames the bare 'we are' statement that the next word locates, since Arabic needs no verb 'to be' in the present.
A preposition meaning 'in' fused with a 'it' pronoun, meaning 'in it'. The pronoun points back to the state named by the relative word before, closing the 'the state we are in' clause in one word.
A particle reopening the rhetorical, urging question, 'do you not...?'. Repeated here, it stacks a second appeal onto the first, keeping the pleading tone over the following clause.
A present-tense verb with 'you' (singular) inside it, meaning to see. The subject is carried in the verb, and under the urging particle before it the sense is again 'do you not see'.

A relative word meaning 'what / that which', here naming what has befallen the speakers. It is the object of the seeing verb and opens a clause completed by the verb after it, standing in for the unspecified events.

A past-tense verb with a 'us' pronoun fused on as its object, meaning 'reached us'. The thing that arrives is the hidden subject, while the attached 'us' is the one overtaken, so the speakers are the receivers.
A particle framing the next words as an urging, rhetorical question, 'will you not...?'. It expects agreement rather than information and turns the clause into a plea for help.
A present-tense verb with 'you' (singular) built into its shape, meaning to intercede. The subject is inside the verb, and under the urging particle before it the sense is 'won't you intercede'.
The preposition li- 'for' fused with a 'us' pronoun, marking who the interceding would benefit. The whole 'for us' is one word, the attached pronoun pointing to the pleading group.
A preposition meaning 'to/toward' that marks the one the intercession is addressed before, putting the following noun in the genitive. It links the act of interceding to the Lord it is brought to.

A noun with a 'your' (singular) pronoun fused onto its end, a possessive in one word. It stands in the genitive because the preposition before it governs that ending, and the attached 'your' stresses the addressee's own bond with his Lord.

The connector fa- 'so/then' fused to a present-tense verb. Fa- moves the narration to this reply, and the verb carries 'he' inside it, so the single word means 'then he says' and opens the quoted speech.

An emphasis particle that underlines the certainty of the coming statement and grabs the following noun into the accusative. Its job is to assert 'it is truly the case that...', which is why the next word takes that ending.

A noun with a 'my' pronoun fused onto its end, a possessive in one word. It sits in the accusative because the emphasis particle before it governs that ending, and the attached 'my' marks the speaker's own Lord.
A past-tense verb with 'he' built into its shape, the predicate of the emphatic sentence, meaning he grew angry. The subject is carried inside, reporting the Lord's anger as a completed event.
A time noun made definite by al- 'the', set in the accusative to work as a 'when' adverb: 'today'. The accusative is what lets a noun pin down the time of the action without a preposition.

A noun in the accusative echoing the verb's own root, used to intensify it, much as English might say 'angry with a great anger'. This cognate accusative underscores the weight and singularity of the anger.

A negation particle that pushes a present-tense verb into past meaning and clips its ending into the shortened jussive form. The clipped ending on the next verb is the fingerprint this negator leaves, giving a past-negative sense.

A present-tense verb with 'he' inside it, pulled into the past and shortened (jussive) by the negation word before it. The sense is 'he never grew angry', the clipped ending marking the negator's effect.
A time noun meaning 'before it' with an 'it' pronoun fused on. The attached pronoun reaches back to the anger just named, setting this anger against everything that came before.

A comparison noun meaning 'its like' with an 'it' pronoun fused on. It says no equal anger existed, the attached 'it' pointing back to the anger named earlier, measuring all other anger against this one.

Two pieces fused: the linking wa- 'and' plus a negation particle that points to the future. Wa- joins this to the previous clause, and the negator denies the coming verb, extending the claim forward in time.

A present-tense verb with 'he' inside it, here aimed at the future and made negative by the particle before it: 'nor will he grow angry'. That future-negation particle also shifts the verb's ending, the trace it leaves on the form.
A time noun meaning 'after it' with an 'it' pronoun fused on. The attached pronoun points to the anger, closing the comparison off on the future side: no anger like it will come later.
A comparison noun meaning 'its like' with an 'it' pronoun fused on, repeated to balance the earlier one. It again denies any equal anger, the attached 'it' pointing back to the anger named before.

Two pieces fused: the linking wa- 'and' plus the emphasis particle carrying a 'he/it' pronoun on its end. Wa- adds a fresh statement, and the emphasis particle drives home its certainty while grabbing its pronoun into the accusative.
A certainty particle that, paired with the past verb sense to come, stresses the action really took place. It leans the statement toward 'indeed there was', adding force rather than new content.

A past 'was' form carrying a feminine ending that agrees with the feminine noun it introduces. This verb sets up an existence statement, 'there was...', leading into the 'for me a supplication' that follows.

The preposition li- 'for' fused with a 'me' pronoun, marking who the supplication belonged to. In this 'there was for me...' frame the li- phrase carries the possession, so 'for me' does the work of 'I had'.

An indefinite noun (carrying the -un tanwin, not al-) that is the thing said to exist, the subject of the 'there was' verb. Its nominative ending marks it as that subject, and its indefiniteness presents the supplication as one particular, unnamed prayer.

A past-tense verb with an 'I' ending built into its shape, opening a clause that describes the supplication just named. The first-person subject is carried inside the verb, so it reads 'I made (it)', telling what was done with that prayer.

The preposition bi- 'with/by' fused to a feminine 'it' pronoun, meaning he prayed by means of it. The attached pronoun points back to the feminine 'supplication' just mentioned, so it ties this clause to that prayer.

A preposition meaning 'against / upon' that here marks the target a curse-prayer is aimed at, putting the following noun in the genitive. With this verb of invoking, it shows the supplication was called down against someone.

A noun with a 'my' pronoun fused onto its end, a possessive in one word. It stands in the genitive because the preposition before it governs that ending, and the attached 'my' marks the people as the speaker's own.

A noun with a 'my' pronoun fused onto its end, cried out alone as an exclamation of self-concern: 'my own self!'. Standing by itself rather than in a full clause, it voices an urgent plea about saving oneself.
The same self-with-'my' word repeated. Arabic uses bare repetition for intensity, so saying it again piles on the urgency, much as English would by simply doubling the word.
A third repeat of the self-with-'my' word, driving the intensity to its peak. The threefold repetition is the grammatical device carrying the emphasis, with no extra particle needed.
A command-form verb addressed to a group, meaning 'go (you all)'. The plural ending marks who is ordered, and as an imperative it gives a direct instruction rather than describing an action.
A preposition meaning 'to/toward' marking the destination of the going, putting the following noun in the genitive. It links the command to leave with the one they are sent to.

A noun meaning 'other than' with a 'me' pronoun fused on, so it reads 'someone other than me'. It stands in the genitive after the preposition before it, the attached 'me' being the point of contrast that redirects them away from the speaker.

This is a command aimed at a group, not one person: the plural '-u' ending built into the verb already names the addressees as 'you all', so Arabic needs no separate pronoun the way English would. It launches the whole scene by sending the crowd off toward someone.

A preposition of motion that does two jobs at once: it forces the following name into the form that marks it as the goal, and it labels that name as the destination the going is aimed at. English splits this into 'to' plus a noun; Arabic ties the case to the preposition itself.

A proper name standing as the goal of the preceding 'to'. Because the preposition governs it, the name takes the ending that marks a noun ruled by a preposition, even though foreign names often resist case changes; here it sits as the target of the motion.

The prefix 'fa-' is a sequencing link meaning the next event follows on from the first command, and the '-una' ending packs in the subject 'they' plus marks this as an ongoing/present action, so one word carries both the connector and the full 'they do X' clause.

The name repeats as the object of the coming-to: Arabic often restates the full noun instead of dropping in a pronoun like English 'him', which keeps the reference unmistakable across the chain of verbs.

Again 'fa-' chains this onto the previous verb, marking speech as the next step after they arrive, while the '-una' ending folds in the 'they' subject. So this single word means 'and then they say', connector and clause together.

A call-particle whose only job is to flag that a direct address follows; it puts the listener on notice that the next word is the person being spoken to. English leans on intonation or 'O', but Arabic marks the vocative openly with this particle.

This is the one being called, so it sits in the special address form that follows the call-particle rather than its ordinary sentence form. Naming the addressee directly sets up the appeal that comes next.

A standalone 'you' pronoun used as the subject of a sentence that has no verb: Arabic can equate two things just by placing pronoun and noun side by side, so 'you (are) the Prophet' needs no word for 'are'. The pronoun is stated for emphasis on the addressee.

The first noun of an 'of' possessive pair: it links straight to the divine name after it with no separate word for 'of', and it gives up taking its own 'the', drawing its definiteness instead from the owner that follows.

The owner in the possessive pair, sitting right after its head noun and taking the ending that marks it as the possessor. Two nouns placed back to back like this build 'Prophet of Allah' without any linking word.

The 'wa-' here links a second title onto the first, and the attached '-hu' ties the friend back to Allah as the one whose friend he is. So the word bundles 'and' plus a possessive that points to God, not to the nearest noun.

A preposition that here marks a source or category: it sets up 'from the people of...' and forces the following noun into the form ruled by a preposition. It frames Abraham as belonging to a class rather than naming a literal point of departure.

Head of another possessive pair: 'people' joins directly to 'the earth' to mean 'people of the earth', taking no 'the' of its own and leaning on the following noun for its definiteness. The ending shows it is governed by the preceding 'from'.

The owner half of the pair, so it carries the possessor ending and supplies the definiteness for 'people' before it. Side-by-side placement, not a linking word, is what makes this 'people OF the earth'.
A bare command directed at one person, telling Abraham to intercede; the imperative shape itself carries the 'you (do it)' without any pronoun. It pivots the address from praise into a request.
A preposition fused with 'us': the one word marks who benefits from the interceding. The preposition assigns a beneficiary role, so this functions as 'on behalf of us' rather than a destination.

Here this motion-preposition is stretched to mean 'toward/with' the Lord as the party the plea is carried to; it forces the following noun into the preposition-governed form and frames the Lord as the endpoint of the intercession.

The attached '-ka' makes this 'your Lord', binding the lordship to the addressee Abraham; the noun also sits in the form demanded by the preposition before it. One word thus carries noun, possessor, and case.

An opening particle that turns the clause into a pointed rhetorical question and adds a nudge of urgency; it is not really asking for information but pressing the listener to acknowledge their plight. It governs the question that follows.

A present-tense verb with the 'you' subject built into its shape, so no separate pronoun is needed; paired with the questioning particle it becomes 'don't you see'. The present form keeps the seeing live and ongoing.

A connector word standing in for 'the thing that': it opens a relative clause and points ahead to the situation described, letting the following words specify what is being seen without a separate noun. It is the hinge between 'see' and the clause.
A standalone 'we' used as the subject of a verbless relative clause: Arabic states the bare pronoun and lets the following preposition complete the sense, so 'we (are) in it' needs no word for 'are'.

A preposition fused with '-hi', so one short word means 'in it', the '-hi' reaching back to the dire state just referred to rather than to any nearby thing. Tracking what that suffix points to is part of reading the line.
A command to a group, with the plural '-u' ending built in to name 'you all' as the addressees; the imperative shape alone carries the order to set off. It sends the crowd toward the next prophet.

A motion-preposition doing double duty: it forces the following name into its governed form and marks that name as the goal the going aims at. Arabic binds the case to the preposition rather than to a separate word.
A proper name serving as the goal of 'to'; foreign names like this resist visible case change, but grammatically it sits as the target the preposition governs. It is the destination of the command.

The 'fa-' marks this as the next step after the order, and the '-una' ending packs in the 'they' subject plus the present reading, so the word means 'and then they come'. Connector and clause travel together.
The name repeats as the one reached, Arabic preferring a restated noun over a pronoun like 'him' to keep the reference clear through the run of verbs. It is the object of the coming.
Again 'fa-' chains the speaking onto their arrival, while the '-una' ending carries the 'they' subject, giving 'and then they say' in one word. The sequencing prefix keeps the events in order.
A call-particle that signals a direct address is coming and flags the next word as the person spoken to. Arabic marks the vocative openly with this particle where English might just use 'O' or tone.
The addressee being called, so it sits in the special form that follows the call-particle rather than its plain sentence form. Naming him directly opens the appeal to him.

A standalone 'you' acting as subject of a verbless equation: 'you (are) the Messenger' needs no word for 'are', since Arabic equates two things by placing them side by side. The pronoun adds weight to the addressee.

The first noun of an 'of' pair: it joins straight to the divine name after it with no separate 'of', and it forgoes its own 'the', taking its definiteness from the owner that follows. This builds 'Messenger of Allah'.
The owner half of the pair, carrying the possessor ending and lending definiteness to 'Messenger' before it; back-to-back placement is what yields 'Messenger OF Allah' with no linking word.
A past verb with '-ka' fused on as its object 'you', so one word means 'He favoured you'; the doer 'Allah' comes next as a stated subject. The attached '-ka' is the receiver of the favouring.
The divine name as the stated subject of the preceding verb, placed after it in the order Arabic favours (verb then doer). Its ending marks it as the one performing the favouring.

The prefix 'bi-' marks the means ('with/by'), and the attached '-hi' makes the messages 'His', pointing back to Allah; the noun also sits in the form that preposition governs. So the word is 'with His messages', instrument plus possessor.

'wa-' adds a second instrument, 'bi-' again marks it as the means, and '-hi' ties the speech back to Allah; one word stacks 'and with His speech'. The chain of prefixes and suffix all hang on this single noun.

A preposition meaning 'over/above', here marking comparison or rank: it forces the following noun into its governed form and frames the people as those the messenger is set above. The preposition assigns the 'over' relationship.
The noun governed by 'over', carrying 'the' and the ending the preposition demands; it names the group the favour raises him above. Definiteness here points to humankind as a whole.
A bare singular command, the imperative shape carrying its own 'you (do it)' with no pronoun, asking Moses to intercede. It turns the praise into the actual request.
A preposition fused with 'us', marking who gains from the interceding; the preposition assigns a beneficiary role, so this is 'on our behalf' rather than a destination.

This motion-preposition is stretched to 'toward/with', naming the Lord as the party the plea is carried to and forcing the following noun into its governed form. It frames the Lord as the endpoint of the appeal.
The attached '-ka' makes this 'your Lord', binding the lordship to Moses; the noun also takes the form the preceding preposition requires. Noun, possessor and case ride on one word.
An opening particle that frames the clause as a pressing rhetorical question rather than a real query, leaning on the listener to admit their state. It governs the question that follows.
A present verb with the 'you' subject built into its shape, so no separate pronoun is needed; with the questioning particle it reads 'don't you see'. The present keeps the seeing immediate.

A connector standing for 'the thing that': it opens a relative clause and points ahead to the situation, letting the following words spell out what is seen without naming a separate noun. It hinges 'see' to the clause.

A preposition fused with '-hi' for 'in it', the '-hi' reaching back to the desperate state just described rather than to any nearby noun. Tracking that referent is part of reading the line.

A motion-preposition that forces the following name into its governed form and marks it as the goal; Arabic ties the case to the preposition rather than a separate word. It points the going at its target.
A proper name as the goal of 'to'; the long final vowel stays put and the name resists visible case change, but grammatically it is the destination the preposition governs.

Again 'fa-' chains the speaking onto their arrival and '-una' carries the 'they' subject, so the word is 'then they say'. The sequencing prefix keeps the order of events.
A call-particle flagging that a direct address follows and marking the next word as the one spoken to; Arabic states the vocative openly here.
The addressee being called, sitting in the special form that follows the call-particle; naming him directly opens the appeal.
A standalone 'you' as subject of a verbless equation: 'you (are) the Messenger' needs no word for 'are', since Arabic equates by juxtaposition. The pronoun stresses the addressee.
The first noun of an 'of' pair, joining straight to the divine name with no separate 'of' and forgoing its own 'the', taking definiteness from the owner that follows. This builds 'Messenger of God'.
The owner half of the pair, carrying the possessor ending and lending definiteness to 'Messenger' before it; side-by-side placement yields 'Messenger OF God' with no linking word.
'wa-' links a new clause and the attached '-hu' makes the word 'His', pointing back to God as the one whose word it is; one word holds 'and His word'. The suffix tracks God, not the nearest noun.
A past verb with '-ha' fused on as its object 'it' (feminine, the 'word'), so the word is 'He cast it'; the 'he' subject is inside the verb. The suffix carries the thing cast, not the recipient.
A motion-preposition marking the recipient: it forces the following name into its governed form and frames her as where the word was cast. The preposition assigns the goal role.
A proper name as the recipient governed by the preceding 'into'; the ending marks it as ruled by that preposition. She is the endpoint of the casting.

'wa-' adds a further description and the noun stays indefinite, no 'the', so it reads 'and a spirit', presenting something unspecified rather than a known one. The bareness is what signals 'a' over 'the'.
A preposition fused with '-hu' for 'from Him', the '-hu' pointing back to God as the source; the one word marks origin. The suffix tracks God across the clause, not a nearby noun.

A past verb in a doubled-middle (intensive) pattern that means 'spoke to' rather than plain 'said', read here with a 'you' subject; the form's strengthened middle is what gives the sense of addressing people directly.

A definite noun in the object form: the 'the' is built on the front and the ending marks it as what the verb acts on, so 'the people' are those spoken to. Definiteness and case both sit on the one word.
A location-preposition that forces the following noun into its governed form and frames it as the place; it sets up the 'in (the cradle)' phrase. The preposition assigns the locative role.
The noun governed by 'in', carrying 'the' and the ending the preposition demands; it names the setting of the speaking. Whether literal cradle or figurative infancy, grammatically it is the place.
A bare singular command, the imperative shape carrying its own 'you (do it)', asking the addressee to intercede. It pivots from the praise into the request.
A preposition fused with 'us', marking who benefits from the interceding; the preposition assigns the beneficiary role, so this is 'on our behalf'.
A motion-preposition stretched to 'toward/with', naming the Lord as the party the plea is carried to and forcing the following noun into its governed form. It frames the Lord as the endpoint.
The attached '-ka' makes this 'your Lord', binding lordship to the addressee; the noun also takes the form the preposition requires. Possessor and case ride on one word.
An opening particle framing the clause as a pressing rhetorical question, leaning on the listener to admit their plight rather than seeking real information. It governs the question that follows.
A present verb with the 'you' subject built in, so no separate pronoun is needed; with the questioning particle it reads 'don't you see'. The present keeps the seeing immediate.
A connector standing for 'the thing that': it opens a relative clause and points ahead to the situation, letting the following words spell out what is seen without a separate noun.
A standalone 'we' subject of a verbless relative clause: the bare pronoun plus the following preposition finishes the sense, so 'we (are) in it' needs no 'are'.
A preposition fused with '-hi' for 'in it', the '-hi' reaching back to the state just described rather than a nearby noun. Tracking that referent is part of reading the line.
The 'fa-' here is a loose linking particle joining this speech to the foregoing, and the present-tense shape carries the 'he' subject and can stand for the future; so the word is 'then he says'.
A proper name, the stated subject of the preceding 'says'; the conventional long-vowel spelling marks it, and as a foreign name it resists visible case change. It identifies who speaks.
An emphasis-particle bracing the coming statement as certain and weighty, and forcing the next noun into a special governed form. Its job is conviction, beyond its 'indeed' gloss.
'Lord' with '-i' fused on for 'my', tying lordship to the speaker; because the emphasis-particle precedes it, the noun also sits in that particle's required form.
A past-form verb naming entry into anger, with the 'he' subject built in; though past in shape it is read here as a present state. The subject rides inside the verb.
A time-word in the adverb form pinning the anger to 'today'; the special ending flags it as a when. It anchors the verb to the present day.
This noun echoes 'was angry' and sits in the object form to intensify it, the Arabic device of reinforcing a verb with its own related noun. The sense is 'angry with a real anger', stressing degree.
A negating particle that turns the following verb into a clipped past-negative and trims its ending; here it opens 'the like of which He never...'. Its grammatical work is negation.
Present in shape but, under the preceding negator, read as a past denial with a shortened ending and the 'he' subject inside. Negator plus clipped form yields 'He never got angry'.
A time-noun fused with '-hu' for 'before it', the suffix pointing back to the anger; the adverb form marks a point in time. The exact thing the suffix points to has to be read from context.
'Like' fused with '-hu' for 'its like', the suffix reaching back to the anger; the word makes a comparison and its ending shows it governed in the clause. It says the anger had no equal.

'wa-' adds a clause and 'lan' inside it is a strong future negator: together they push the denial forward, 'and never will...'. This negator specifically rules out the future and reshapes the verb after it.
Driven by the future-negator before it, this present verb takes the lighter ending that negator forces and reads 'will (never) be angry'; the 'he' subject is inside. Mood comes from the particle.
A time-noun with an attached '-hi' for 'after it', the suffix tied to the singular anger; the form marks a point in time. It seals off the future to match 'before it'.
'Like' plus '-hu' once more for 'its like', repeated to bracket the comparison on the future side, the suffix pointing to the same anger. The full word repeats rather than a lone pronoun.
'wa-' adds a clause and 'lam' inside it is a past-negator that clips the following verb's ending; together 'and He did not...'. The negator's job is to deny a past action.
A present-shaped verb forced by the preceding negator into a past-negative with a shortened ending, the 'he' subject inside; so 'he did not mention'. Negator plus this form is how Arabic says it.

An indefinite noun in the object form, the thing not mentioned; the lack of 'the' under negation gives 'any sin at all', and the ending marks it as the verb's object. Indefinite-under-negation widens it to 'any'.
A noun fused with '-i' for 'my self', cried out alone with no verb as a bare appeal for himself; the first of three repeats begins the rising emotional drumbeat through sheer reiteration.
The same self-cry repeated, the '-i' still meaning 'my'; with no verb it stands as raw exclamation. The second beat intensifies the self-concern by restating the whole word.
The third self-cry, '-i' again 'my', stacking the repetition to a peak; Arabic conveys mounting urgency by reiterating the bare word rather than adding intensifiers. It caps the emotional climb.
A plural command, the '-u' ending naming the whole crowd as addressees and the imperative carrying 'you (go)'; it turns them away to seek help elsewhere.
A motion-preposition forcing the following word into its governed form and marking it the destination; here it points the crowd onward. Case and direction ride on the preposition.
'Other-than' fused with '-i' for 'other than me', the suffix excluding the speaker; idiomatically 'someone else'. The attached pronoun carves 'me' out of the field of helpers.
A plural command repeated, the '-u' ending again naming the crowd as addressees and the imperative carrying 'you (go)'; the restated command now sends them on to the final prophet.
A motion-preposition forcing the following name into its governed form and marking it the destination; it ties the command to where they must head next.
A proper name as the object of the preceding 'to', taking the ending that marks a noun ruled by a preposition; the visible final mark is its case ending as the destination. He is where they are sent.
A past verb opening the set blessing-formula on the Prophet; it pairs with the following 'upon him' and 'peace' verb to make the fixed honorific. As a formula it stays short and conventional.
The divine name as the stated subject of the blessing-verb, placed after it in Arabic's verb-then-doer order; its ending marks it as the one sending the blessing. Part of the fixed honorific.
A preposition fused with '-hi' for 'upon him', the '-hi' pointing to the Prophet as the one blessed; it names who the blessing falls on within the formula.
'wa-' links the second half of the honorific and the doubled-middle verb means 'grant peace'; together with the blessing-verb it completes the set salawat formula. Conventional and kept brief.

'wa-' opens the clause and is welded onto the location-preposition 'in', so the one word is 'and in'; the preposition then forces the following noun into its governed form. Connector and preposition share the word.
An indefinite noun governed by the preceding 'in', so it carries the form that preposition demands and stays without 'the', giving 'in a report' rather than a specific one. Bareness signals 'a'.

The 'fa-' marks the next step, the '-una' ending carries the 'they' subject, and '-ni' fused at the end is the object 'me'; so one word means 'then they come to me'. Prefix, subject and object all on one verb.
Again 'fa-' chains the speaking onto their coming, and '-una' carries the 'they' subject, giving 'then they say'. The sequencing prefix keeps the events in order.
A call-particle flagging a direct address and marking the next word as the one spoken to; Arabic states the vocative openly here.
The addressee being called, in the special form that follows the call-particle; the visible final mark is the address-form ending. Naming him directly opens the speech.

The owner half of the pair, carrying the possessor ending and lending definiteness to 'Messenger' before it; juxtaposition yields 'Messenger OF God'.

'wa-' adds a second title and the noun 'Seal' heads a fresh 'of' pair with the following 'prophets'; the word bundles 'and' plus the head of that possessive chain. Two titles are linked by the prefix.
The owner closing the 'Seal of the prophets' pair: a definite plural carrying the possessor ending and supplying definiteness to 'Seal' before it. Side-by-side placement builds the 'of' link.

'wa-' opens a new clause and the small particle fused after it sharpens the coming passive verb into a settled 'and indeed (it) has...'; the particle affirms the action truly occurred. It frames the forgiveness clause.

A passive past verb: the inner vowels mark forgiveness as something received, not done, so the sins are the thing forgiven and no doer is named. Arabic builds the passive by reshaping the vowels rather than adding a helper word.
A preposition fused with '-ka' for 'for you', marking the Prophet as the one in whose favour the forgiving happened; the preposition assigns the beneficiary role. One word for two English words.
A connector standing for 'that which': it opens a relative clause and serves as the real subject of the passive 'was forgiven', pointing ahead to the sins the following verbs describe.
A past verb meaning 'went before', with a built-in 'it' subject pointing back to the 'what' just named; it specifies that part of the forgiven sins which came earlier. The subject is carried inside.

A preposition marking the category drawn from, here 'of your sin', forcing the following noun into its governed form; it frames the 'what preceded' as a portion of the sins. The preposition sets the partitive sense.
A noun fused with '-ka' for 'your sin', binding the sin to the Prophet; the noun also sits in the form the preceding preposition governs. Possessor and case on one word.
'wa-' adds a parallel clause and the connector after it stands for 'that which', opening a second relative; together 'and what (came after)'. It balances the earlier 'what preceded'.

A past verb meaning 'came after', with a built-in 'it' subject pointing back to the second 'what'; it names the later part of the forgiven sins, mirroring the earlier 'preceded'. Subject inside the verb.
A bare singular command, the imperative shape carrying its own 'you (do it)', asking the addressee to intercede. It opens the request directly.
A preposition fused with 'us', marking who benefits from the interceding; the preposition assigns the beneficiary role, so 'on our behalf'.
A motion-preposition stretched to 'toward/with', naming the Lord as the party the plea is carried to and forcing the following noun into its governed form. It frames the Lord as the endpoint.

The 'fa-' marks the result/next step ('so'), and the present-tense first-person verb carries the 'I' subject inside it; so the word is 'so I set out'. Connector and 'I'-clause travel together.
Again 'fa-' chains this onto the previous action, and the first-person present verb folds in the 'I' subject, giving 'so I come'. The sequencing prefix orders the steps of the vision.

A place-preposition that forces the following noun into its governed form and frames it as the location beneath which he arrives; it sets up 'beneath the Throne'. The preposition assigns the locative role.
A definite noun governed by 'beneath', carrying 'the' and the ending the preposition demands; it names the Throne as the place. Definiteness and case both on the one word.
Once more 'fa-' chains the next action and the first-person present verb carries the 'I' subject, so 'so I fall'. The prefix keeps the prostration in sequence with the arrival.

A descriptive word in the object form used to tell the manner of the falling, 'falling (while) prostrate'; the special ending is what marks it as describing how, not as a thing acted on. It colours the verb.

The prefix 'li-' marks direction or devotion 'to/before', and '-i' fused on makes it 'my Lord'; the noun sits in the form that prefix governs. So one word is 'before my Lord', with the possessor attached.

A sequencing particle stronger than plain 'and', marking a clear step-after with a gap, 'then'; it orders the next event as distinctly following. Unlike 'fa-', it suggests a more separated next stage.
A present-tense verb with a built-in 'he' subject, the doer (God) stated as a separate word right after; the present keeps the opening-up vivid and ongoing. The subject sits inside until named.
The divine name as the stated subject of the preceding verb, placed after it in Arabic's verb-then-doer order; its ending marks it as the one who opens. It identifies the actor.
A preposition fused with '-ya' for 'upon me', the '-ya' naming the speaker as the one the opening is granted to; it marks the recipient. One word for two English words.
A partitive preposition introducing 'some of', forcing the following noun into its governed form and framing the praises as a portion rather than the whole. The preposition sets the 'part of' sense.
A plural noun fused with '-hi' for 'His praises', the '-hi' pointing back to God; the noun also sits in the form the preceding partitive preposition governs. Possessor and case on one word.
The 'fa-' marks the next step ('so/then') and the first-person present verb carries the 'I' subject inside it, giving 'so I raise'. Connector and 'I'-clause together.
A noun fused with '-i' for 'my head', the '-i' the possessor, sitting as the object of the raising; one word holds noun and possessor. It names what is lifted.
Again 'fa-' chains the speaking onto the raising and the first-person present verb folds in the 'I' subject, so 'so I say'. The prefix keeps the actions in sequence.
A noun fused with '-i' for 'my community', the '-i' the possessor; cried out alone it is a bare appeal on their behalf, no verb needed. The suffix binds the community to the speaker.
A call-particle flagging a direct address to the Lord that follows; it marks the next word as the one being called. Arabic states the vocative openly.
'Lord' fused with a possessor for 'my Lord', in the shortened address-form that follows the call-particle; the suffix ties lordship to the speaker as he appeals. Calling on God directly.
The community-cry repeats, '-i' still 'my'; with no verb it stands as raw appeal, the restatement pressing the plea for them. Repetition is how the urgency builds.
The call-particle again flags a renewed direct address to the Lord, marking the next word as the one called; the repeat underscores the pleading. Stated openly as before.
'My Lord' once more in the address-form after the call-particle, the suffix again tying lordship to the speaker; the second call reinforces the appeal on the community's behalf.

The 'fa-' links this to the foregoing and the verb is an impersonal passive, 'it will be said', with no named speaker: the passive vowels leave the sayer open so the message stands forward. Connector plus passive on one word.
A call-particle flagging a direct address and marking the next word as the one spoken to; Arabic states the vocative openly here.
The addressee being called, in the special form that follows the call-particle; naming him directly opens the command. The final mark is the address-form ending.

A causative command (an 'admit/cause to enter' pattern) carrying its own 'you (do it)'; the form's shape turns 'enter' into 'make enter', so it is an order to bring others in. The 'you' lives in the verb.
A partitive preposition introducing 'some from among', forcing the following noun into its governed form and framing the community as the pool drawn from. The preposition sets the 'part of' sense.
A noun fused with '-ka' for 'your community', the '-ka' the possessor; the noun also sits in the form the preceding partitive preposition governs. Possessor and case on one word.
A connector standing for 'those who': it opens a relative clause naming a sub-group of the community, the ones the following words describe. It is the hinge to that clause.
A negating particle denying the following phrase; here it sets up 'no reckoning (is) upon them'. Its job is to negate the existence of the thing named next.

A noun in the object form built into a 'there is no X' negation: paired with the negator it means 'no reckoning'; the special ending is the mark this fixed negation pattern requires. It denies any reckoning for them.
A preposition fused with '-him' for 'upon them', the '-him' pointing back to that sub-group; it completes 'no reckoning upon them'. One word for two English words, tracking the just-named people.

A partitive/source preposition marking 'through (one) of', forcing the following noun into its governed form; here it frames the gate as the route of entry. The preposition assigns the 'by way of' sense.
A definite noun governed by the preceding preposition, carrying 'the' and its required ending; it names the gate as the route. It is then specified by the describing word that follows.

A describing word agreeing with 'the gate' before it, carrying its own 'the' to match, so it reads 'the right-hand (gate)'; Arabic makes an adjective echo its noun's definiteness and case. It pins down which gate.

A partitive preposition opening 'of the gates', forcing the following noun into its governed form and framing the right-hand gate as one drawn from the set. The preposition sets the 'one of' relation.

The first noun of an 'of' pair, 'gates', joining straight to 'Paradise' with no separate 'of' and forgoing its own 'the', taking definiteness from the owner that follows; it also sits in the form the preceding preposition governs.
The owner half of the pair, carrying the possessor ending and lending definiteness to 'gates' before it; juxtaposition builds 'gates OF Paradise' with no linking word.

'wa-' opens a new clause and the attached pronoun is a standalone 'they', subject of a verbless 'they (are) sharers'; the prefix joins the clause while the pronoun, stated openly, points back to that admitted group.

A plural noun acting as the predicate of 'they (are)', so 'they are partners/sharers'; with no verb the equation is made by placing pronoun and noun together. It heads the 'sharers of the people' sense.
The owner half of an 'of' pair with 'sharers', so 'sharers of the people'; the noun carries the possessor ending and lends definiteness to the word before it. Juxtaposition makes the link.

A location-preposition fused with the connector 'what', giving 'in that which', and it opens a relative clause; the preposition forces the relative content into its governed frame. One word fuses preposition and relative.

A noun meaning 'other than/besides' that heads an 'of' link with the following 'that', forcing it into the governed form; it frames the remaining gates as everything apart from the named one. It sets the 'beyond that' contrast.

A pointing word 'that', the owner closing the 'other than that' link and pointing back to the right-hand gate just mentioned; it carries the form that preceding word governs. It anchors the contrast to a known referent.
A partitive preposition opening 'of the gates', forcing the following noun into its governed form and framing the rest as drawn from the wider set. The preposition sets the 'among' relation.

A definite plural governed by the preceding preposition, carrying 'the' and its required ending; it names the remaining gates the group shares with others. Definiteness here points to the rest of the known set.
A sequencing particle meaning 'then', marking a clear step-after that moves the narration to a new statement; stronger than plain 'and', it sets this oath apart as a distinct next stage.
A past verb with a built-in 'he' subject, introducing the speech that follows; Arabic carries the subject inside the verb, so no separate 'he' is needed. It opens the reported oath.

'wa-' here is the special oath-'by', not plain 'and': it swears by what follows and forces that following phrase into the form an oath governs. Its job is to open a solemn vow, beyond any 'and' reading.
A noun fused with '-i' for 'my self/soul', heading the oath-phrase 'the One in whose hand is my soul'; the suffix ties the soul to the speaker. It is the thing said to be in God's hand.
The prefix 'bi-' marks 'in (the) hand' and '-hi' makes it 'His hand', pointing back to the One sworn by; the noun sits in the form that prefix governs. One word holds 'in', 'hand' and 'His'.
An emphasis-particle bracing the coming statement as certain and weighty, and forcing the next noun into a special governed form; here it opens the content of the oath. Its job is conviction.

A connector standing for 'that which/the thing that': it acts as the subject of the coming comparison, pointing ahead to the distance described; the following preposition then measures it. It anchors 'what (is) between'.

A preposition meaning 'between' that, by its nature, looks for two items to span; it forces the following noun into its governed form and sets up the gap measured. Here it frames the distance between the two panels.

A dual noun, Arabic's dedicated 'exactly two' form: the ending itself carries 'two panels', so no separate word for 'two' is needed; it also takes the form 'between' governs. The count rides on the word's shape.

A partitive preposition opening 'of the leaves/panels', forcing the following noun into its governed form and framing the two panels as part of Paradise's gates. The preposition sets the 'of' relation.

The first noun of an 'of' pair, joining straight to 'Paradise' with no separate 'of' and forgoing its own 'the', taking definiteness from the owner that follows; it also sits in the form the preceding preposition governs.
The owner half of the pair, carrying the possessor ending and lending definiteness to 'gates' before it; juxtaposition builds 'gates OF Paradise' with no linking word.
A comparison-word fused from 'like' plus 'what', giving 'just as'; it opens the yardstick clause that measures the distance. The fusion is what makes one word do 'as/like that which'.

'Between' again, by nature spanning two points and forcing the following noun into its governed form; here it sets up the measured gap between two cities. The preposition frames the comparison's distance.
A city-name as the first point of the 'between' span; though a place-name it takes the form the preposition governs, marking it as one end of the measured distance. It anchors the comparison.
